transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-03
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Lena Park (CTO, Northridge), Samir Patel (Lead Eng), Evelyn Cruz (PM)

Summary:
Quick hosted API onramp focused on streaming behavior, parameter smoothing (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and retry/backoff best practices. Customer concerned about latencies at tail, cost trade-offs, and safe fallbacks for occasional model failures. Agreed to run short pilot and share param presets + benchmark results.

Topics:
- Streaming chunking and partial responses
- Temperature / top_p / max_new_tokens presets for customer use cases (support chat + short summarization)
- Idempotency and retries (exponential backoff, safe dedupe)
- Console observability: token breakdown, per-route latency, and traces
- Optimize recommendations: batching, prefix caching, fallback models

Action items (captured in metadata; partial recitation here): see action items above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — we'll do a quick hosted API onramp today, focus on streaming, parameter ideas, and how retries look in practice. Daniel's got a short demo.
[00:12] Lena Park: Thanks Maya. We're under some time pressure — we want to roll this into a pilot with our support chat flow. Main concerns: latency under load, occasional timeouts, and cost.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Totally. That's exactly what we see. Daniel — want to kick off with a quick stream demo and then we'll map to their traffic?
[00:28] Daniel Ortiz: Yeah sure. I'll share a couple of example requests. Quick note — I might mispronounce some internal names, sorry if that sounds off.
[00:36] Daniel Ortiz: So first: streaming behavior. When you hit the hosted chat endpoint, tokens come as small chunks. For short responses you'll usually see 1-3 chunks, for longer ones many more. The important part is handling partial deltas — we surface the partial text as it arrives so UI can render progressively.
[00:52] Samir Patel: When a chunk drops or the connection resets for a user, what's the recommended client behavior? Do we re-request with last token id or replay?
[01:01] Daniel Ortiz: Good question. For streaming we recommend idempotent replays at the message level. Aka, include a client-side message id for each user message. If there's an abrupt disconnect, you can reissue the same request with the same id and Redwood will route to the model; on hosted we don't persist full KV caches for long-term per-session unless you opt into prefix caching. So you either resume by re-sending the message or do a short tail-replay. Avoid naively resending many times — use exponential backoff.
[01:25] Lena Park: So we would need to implement the dedupe id on our side. That's fine. What about partial tokens appearing twice if we reconnect?
[01:33] Daniel Ortiz: Client should be built to handle dedupe on deltas — easiest is to re-render based on message id and sequence number. We also expose a message-level status in the console and traces so you can correlate.
[01:44] Evelyn Cruz: For our use case, summaries are often short — mostly 20-80 tokens. What are best defaults for temperature and top_p for deterministic replies?
[01:52] Daniel Ortiz: For deterministic short replies we suggest temperature 0.0-0.3 and top_p around 0.8-1.0 depending on how much sampling you want. Max_new_tokens you control per call — for 20-80 tokens set a cap around 128 to be safe. Lower temp reduces creativity but can increase repetition risk; top_p gives a softer knob.
[02:12] Samir Patel: Any smart presets or "smoothing" patterns you recommend? We get weird truncation if the model switches mid-sentence.
[02:19] Maya Chen: We call some of our recommended presets "smoothing" — it's basically a combination: start with temp 0.2, top_p 0.9, and use stop tokens to avoid trailing fragments. Also enable partial_delimiter handling on the client so UI waits for punctuation heuristics before finalizing.
[02:36] Daniel Ortiz: Also, for truncation, watch the token budget per call. Use early stopping tokens (like "\nUser:") if you have structured outputs. For conversational continuity, prefix caching helps — Redwood Optimize recommends prefix caching when the same conversation histories are reused frequently. That reduces latency and cost.
[02:54] Lena Park: Prefix caching — is that something enabled on hosted by default?
[02:58] Daniel Ortiz: It's opt-in per route. We can enable it for your pilot. It stores KV cache entries for short-lived sessions; default TTL is short to avoid retention issues, and it's configurable.
[03:10] Evelyn Cruz: Security: we have to keep everything in vendor-passed logs for compliance. What telemetry do you retain from streaming requests?
[03:18] Maya Chen: We surface per-request token counts, latencies, and traces in the console. For hosted, we keep aggregated traces and can export detailed logs to your SIEM. If you need no retention, you'd want Redwood Private, but for most pilot flows hosted with restricted retention and encryption-in-transit+at-rest covers it. We'll send our SOC 2 + security whitepaper.
[03:37] Samir Patel: Competitors like OpenAI don't give the same per-route breakdowns we liked your console screenshots. Good to know.
[03:43] Maya Chen: Right, our console breaks latency down by model, queue wait, and tokenization time.
[03:49] Daniel Ortiz: Back to retries — typical pattern is: first try immediate retry for 429 up to 1-2 times, then exponential backoff 0.5s, 1s, 2s with jitter. For streaming partial failures, if you get an intermediate error code, don't attempt to stitch partial deltas client-side without dedupe ids, instead re-request the same message id.
[04:10] Samir Patel: For heavy loads we anticipate bursts up to 3x normal traffic. How do you handle burst throttling?
[04:16] Daniel Ortiz: Hosted has a per-account rate limit with burst allowances. You can request higher quotas for the pilot. If you're sensitive to tail latency, we can also set routing to prioritize lower-latency model variants — slightly higher cost but better SLOs.
[04:31] Lena Park: Cost — can you ballpark cost difference if we move from temp 0.0 to 0.7 with more sampling?
[04:36] Maya Chen: Sampling itself doesn't change token count much unless you increase max_new_tokens. But higher temp often leads to longer responses and sometimes more regeneration attempts if not constrained. We can show cost delta with a small traffic sample — that's part of the spreadsheet we'll send.
[04:49] Evelyn Cruz: Show us the retry examples in the console; maybe this is a good time for a short live playthrough?
[04:55] Daniel Ortiz: Sure — demo mode. I'm going to simulate a streaming call and then force a network reset. You should see the partial stream come in, then the client retry with same message id and the server returns the full final.
[05:08] [demo noise — screen share begins, a few seconds of background typing]
[05:20] Daniel Ortiz: Alright here's a short message, temp 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_new_tokens 60. Streaming chunks start — you can see deltas in the UI. Now I kill the socket — one second —
[05:33] Samir Patel: I saw a 3-line partial then reconnect, then a duplicate phrase appeared, small UI hiccup — is that avoidable?
[05:40] Daniel Ortiz: Duplicate phrases are client-side dedupe territory. Our SDKs include helpers that use sequence IDs to merge chunks. If you use a plain websocket implementation you need to implement the check.
[05:50] Lena Park: Do you have official SDKs for our stack? We're mostly Typescript + React on the frontend, Python on backend.
[05:58] Maya Chen: Yes — official JS/TS SDK with streaming helpers, we also have python helpers for server-side. We'll share direct links and example snippets.
[06:06] Evelyn Cruz: For the pilot we want deterministic canned responses for ticket triage plus a summarization microservice. Which model family do you suggest?
[06:14] Daniel Ortiz: For triage, a faster tuned chat model with lower context size is fine. For summarization, a slightly larger model helps for quality. If cost is a concern, use a smaller model with higher temp smoothing and apply reranking for final candidate selection — that keeps unit cost low.
[06:29] Samir Patel: Reranking — do you host that or do we manage?
[06:33] Maya Chen: You can do either. Redwood has an embeddings+rerank path in the platform; we can show how to pipeline generation -> rerank -> final output. For the pilot we can recommend a simple rerank step client-side.
[06:45] Daniel Ortiz: One more note on idempotency headers: include a custom id in the POST body or an x-client-idempotency header. When you reissue, Redwood will try to correlate; hosted correlation window is limited, not a durable transaction log.
[06:58] Lena Park: Understood. On logging retention, do you provide an option to purge after X days?
[07:03] Maya Chen: Yes, we can apply shorter retention windows per route on hosted. For stricter control, our Private offering gives you full control. We'll include both options in the security doc.
[07:12] Evelyn Cruz: Any pitfalls you commonly see in bootstrapping streaming chat?
[07:16] Daniel Ortiz: A few: not deduping deltas leading to double text; not setting reasonable max_tokens leading to runaway costs; not using stop tokens or structured delimiters which makes truncation messy. Also, ignoring retry jitter can create thundering herd during a partial outage.
[07:31] Samir Patel: For the console, can we get per-route SLO alerts? We need to page on high tail latency.
[07:36] Maya Chen: Yes we can configure alerts per route and threshold on p95/p99 latency. We'll include a suggested alerting template in the doc.
[07:45] Daniel Ortiz: Alright, quick recap of recommended starter presets for Northridge: triage chat route — temp 0.0-0.2, top_p 0.8-0.95, max_new_tokens 80, prefix caching enabled for repeated context. Summarizer route — temp 0.2-0.4, top_p 0.9, max_new_tokens 256, rerank final candidates. Retries: 1 immediate retry on 429 or transient network error, then exponential backoff with jitter.
[08:12] Lena Park: Sounds reasonable. We'll review internally and share sample prompts + traffic.
[08:18] Evelyn Cruz: Can you email the SDK links, the param presets, and the pilot calendar invite?
[08:23] Maya Chen: Yep — I'll send SDK links and the presets spreadsheet, Daniel will run the benchmark and attach results. We'll schedule the kickoff for Aug 10 if that works.
[08:33] Samir Patel: Quick question — do you support streaming stop reasons in the API so we can differentiate model-finished vs truncated?
[08:39] Daniel Ortiz: We include a termination reason metadata at the end of the stream: e.g., "stop_token" vs "length_limit" vs "cancelled". That helps instrumentation.
[08:50] Lena Park: Great, that helps for our analytics.
[08:53] Maya Chen: Ok closing notes: action items are in the invite and I'll attach SOC2/security docs. Any other quick Qs?
[08:59] [brief silence]
[09:02] Evelyn Cruz: Nope — that's it for now. Thanks Maya and Daniel.
[09:05] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials. Bye.

End of call.
